PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKER AND MEMBERS OF YUKON TERRITORIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: Two weeks ago this house was honoured by a visit from the members of the council of the Northwest Territories. Today we have in the Speaker's gallery four members of the council of Canada's other far northern territory, the Yukon. In addition to council members John Watt, Donald Taylor and Kenneth Thompson, we have present the Speaker of the Yukon council, Mr. George Shaw. I am sure all hon. members would want me, on their behalf, to extend a very warm welcome to these members of a small but important legislative body that is taking so much responsibility for the growth and development of the Yukon.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKER AND MEMBERS OF YUKON TERRITORIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of personal privilege. Yesteday it was my pleasure to visit the city of Montreal and spend a few hours in that very friendly and warm hearted
community. It was my privilege to speak to the students of Sir George Williams college, but I must confess that during my brief stay there I very soon came to the conclusion they were interested in other matters that had occurred not too far from that spot a few hours earlier.
It was only upon my return, Mr. Speaker, that I discovered there had also been a rather warm, but not so cordial, occurrence in this distinguished House of Commons and that during the course of the discussion my name had become involved in a way that was not as cordial and friendly as that in which it had been involved during my visit to Montreal.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to raise a question of privilege of this kind, even though the matter had been before the house a few days earlier as the result of a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso). I must confess that I had been surprised at the interest of the hon. member for Hamilton West in the very vexing and in many respects unfortunate episode in the history of this parliament concerning the investigation of Chinese immigration cases. The hon. member for Hamilton West was not in the house when those events took place, and I was surprised that he should have expressed an interest in a subject which I thought had been long ago resolved to the mutual satisfaction and with the unanimous agreement of ail members of this house.
However, I am not going to pursue that thought further, because I understand the hon. member for Port Arthur has already indicated that he will be bringing a formal motion before this chamber based on the interest of the hon. member for Hamilton West. All I can say is that I am disappointed that he has been the one who has indulged in activities that revive the shadow of suspicion that has hung over our Chinese community for so long.

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I can sympathize with the Minister of Transport's concern, for I had brought to his attention when he was minister of citizenship and immigration many examples of discrimination in this matter of Chinese immigration. I always tried to be discreet and responsible in these matters because we were dealing with sensitive areas of human relations. The hon. gentleman will remember one case in particular-I think this is what brought out my interest in the subject of Chinese immigration more than anything else-where an unfortunate suicide occurred in the city of Brandon as a result of our discriminatory attitude in matters of this kind.
All I want today is to let the Hansard record speak for itself. As I said at the outset of my statement, anything which was done in respect to the handling of investigations of irregularities in Chinese immigration was done in accordance with definite policy statements made where they should be made, on the floor of the House of Commons, policies which were wholeheartedly acquiesced in by both the present Minister of Justice and by the Minister of Transport and which, as I have indicated, received the wholehearted support of all the members of this house.
I will point out also with regard to the letter which has been brought into question that it was written on August 17 from my home in the city of Brandon at a time when the house was not in session. This is the only means by which a member of parliament can draw the attention of government departments to a local situation as he sees it. This

is what I have always attempted to do in my letters to government officials and government departments. We are aware that it is not possible for members of parliament to telephone; this subject has come up in the house from time to time. We have to resort to the postal service in order to communicate with the people responsible.
The first announcement on this Chinese immigration investigation came on January 19, 1960. As reported at page 83 of Hansard for that date Hon. Ellen Fairclough said:
Mr. Speaker, the alleged illegal entry of persons into Canada from the mainland of China, Macao and Hong Kong has been a matter of grave concern to my department for some time. Early last year I directed that the situation should be thoroughly investigated. A departmental official went from Ottawa to Hong Kong to consult with the British police, and an exhaustive examination of the situation has been in progress for some months in close co-operation with the authorities of the colony.
On June 6, 1960 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate became active in this matter, and as reported on page 4533 of Hansard he demanded a statement of policy from the government. He asserted that reports in the press had cast suspicion on the whole of the Chinese community in Canada, and termed fantastic a report that some 11,000 Chinese had entered the country illegally. In reply to this statement and to a question by the hon. member for Skeena the minister of justice said, in part:
The intention is not to persecute but to establish what are the facts and then do our best to clear up and regularize the situation.
On June 9, 1960 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate speaking again, as reported at page 4716, said as follows:
I am going to recommend to the government, and I am doing this without seeking to be unduly critical, that many of the problems they now have as a result of this investigation could very easily be removed if the minister, the Minister of Justice or the Prime Minister would say, on behalf of the government, that the government has no intention whatever of opening any case or dealing with any case where those people who entered were the sons, daughters, wives or parents of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin, even though they may have misrepresented some of the other facts for which the department asked.
Again, Mr. Speaker, at page 4717:
-it is of the utmost importance that we should make clear at once that so far as those people who are relatives of Chinese Canadian citizens are concerned, who may have committed some technical irregularity in connection with their entry, they are not going to face deportation or any other charges.
Then on June 9, 1960, as reported at page 4722 of Hansard, Hon. Mrs. Fairclough, the then minister, said as follows:
Question of Privilege
-I can assure all members of this house that there is no intention to prosecute those people who are, let us say, victims of these transactions. The intention is rather to curb the activities of the racketeers.
That was on June 9, 1960, Mr. Speaker. I am reciting this Hansard record because it is out of the background of the recommendations made by the Minister of Transport that I wrote the letter to the justice department indicating the situation as I found it when I was able to return to the constituency. The minister of justice was also, of course, involved in policy statements on this matter, and on July 6, 1960, the then minister, Hon. E. D. Fulton, discussed government policy during a supply debate. This is reported at page 5813 of Hansard:
Now, with regard to the whole operation, Mr. Chairman, it must be borne in mind that we are investigating a racket.
Again, at page 5815:
I refer now to persons who are guilty of operating an illegal racket. I am satisfied that when that is established and the Chinese community know that so far as we can we will get these racketeers off their backs, then the feeling of the Chinese community will be one of relief and satisfaction.
And further:
-our intention is to convict racketeers and not to prosecute or harass people who have in many cases committed no more than a technical offence-
On the same page the then minister of justice is reported as having said:
-the minister-
That is the minister of citizenship and immigration:
-has made her stand clear as far as the Chinese are concerned who were what I might call innocent passengers in this vehicle. We are after those who operated the vehicle itself.
A year later, on June 10, 1961, as reported at page 6138 of Hansard, the minister of justice once again referred to government policy in the following terms:
-when the minister-
That is the minister of citizenship and immigration:
-announced the inquiry and the steps that had been taken to date and would be taken in the subsequent period, she said that she counted particularly, in what is described colloquially but somewhat inaccurately as the amnesty program, on the co-operation of the Chinese community to clear those who might be referred to as innocent passengers in this traffic and to establish who are the ringleaders in organized criminal activity.
At page 6139:
The intent of my colleague's statement was to make clear that persons who with respect to themselves or their immediate relatives may have

Question of Privilege
given misinformation in order to bring themselves or their relatives here to Canada, not for the purpose of profit, would not be pushed around or prosecuted.
Hon. Richard Bell took over as minister of citizenship and immigration, and he reiterated the same policy. On November 16, 1962 he announced that the investigation had been concluded and the Hong Kong police would be returning to Hong Kong. I noticed that something has been made of my reference to a police state. I would merely remind hon. members of this house that the Hong Kong police carried out this particular investigation.
In response to the statement made by the new minister, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as recorded at page 1694 of Hansard for 1962-63, he said:
Mr. Speaker, without any qualification I congratulate the new minister on accepting the advice which was tendered from this side of the house two years ago as to the proper method of dealing with this problem. I am very glad indeed that the minister is now removing the shadow that has hung for far too long over the whole Chinese community in Canada-
That policy was accepted and adopted by the new minister of citizenship and immigration under the Liberal government, the man who is now Minister of Justice, who attacked me vehemently yesterday in this chamber. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and all my colleagues in this house, which is the highest court of public opinion in the land and which usually operates with dignity and responsibility, that there was no bribery or coercion involved in any representations I made. I merely wrote a letter to the Department of Justice at a time when I was in my constituency in respect of the attitude of constituents about this particular aspect of a very unhappy situation. I also provided a character reference on behalf of the man concerned. I have written dozens of letters of a similar nature during the 14 years I have been a member of this House of Commons, as no doubt have most the hon. members of this house.
My attention has been drawn to a statement made by one of the oldest members of this house. Perhaps I should not use that term but rather say that he is a man who has been a member of this House of Commons for a lengthy period of time-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-in an answer he gave to a ques-

tion regarding the responsibilities of a member of parliament as a representative of his constituents. That hon. gentleman said that he followed one rule in regard to writing letters to government departments, to the effect that they must be of such a nature that he would not hesitate to have them tabled in the house.

I assure the hon. member that there was no intention on my part to create any-

maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege which appears to involve collusion between officials of the Department of Justice and certain members of parliament, in particular Messrs. Francis, Basford and Macaluso. To illustrate this collusion I should like to make reference to certain questions on the order paper, being questions Nos. 2,042, 2,608, 2,766 and 2,805.
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this question of privilege there seem to be two alternatives open to me. The first involves a formal motion to refer this matter to the standing committee on privileges and elections. The second, which may well be a preliminary to the first, is to suggest that Your Honour take this matter under advisement.
Under the accepted rules of this house the right to ask questions is part of the privileges extended to hon. members of this House of Commons, but as I understand the situation this privilege is not extended in the same way, or at least to the same degree, to members on the government side. It is my belief that when you, sir, and other members of this house read these questions to which I have made reference you will wonder why they were ever accepted. The rules indicate that questions should be framed in such a way as to elicit information rather than give it. These questions appear to me to transgress many of the rules we have in respect of the kind of questions which should be allowed.
I should like to read one of these questions as an example of what I mean, and I shall read question 2,042, which was filed by Mr. Francis on October 2, 1964. The question reads as follows:
1.	Did the Department of Justice, in 1358, through the R.C.M.P., conduct an investigation to determine if Hal Banks had been employing intimidation and violence in the furtherance of union activities?
2.	Did the government on February 23, 1959, as a result of the aforementioned investigation, receive a full account of the conspiracy which resulted in the Walsh beatings?
3.	Was any action taken by the government of that day to bring Banks to trial as a result of that evidence?
4.	Was another report, which included a further account of the Walsh conspiracy, sent on June 14, 1961, to the government by the Department of Justice?
5.	Was any action taken against Banks as a result of that evidence?
6.	On what date was the commission, concerning matters relating to the destruction of shipping on the great lakes, the St. Lawrence river system, and connecting waters, established?
Question of Privilege
7.	When did the commission report?
8.	When was action initiated by the government to prosecute Hal Banks?
Mr. Speaker, it is apparent from the information contained in that question that it is extremely unlikely the hon. member for Carleton had the specified dates and facts at his fingertips.
There have been a number of questions of this kind which have appeared on the order paper recently, the last one being that put forward by Mr. Basford, No. 2,805; and one can only come to the conclusion that someone in the Department of Justice-perhaps the parliamentary secretary-has made a search of the correspondence files and other records for the purpose of planting these questions with government backbenchers in order to embarrass other members of parliament.
There is no reason whatsoever why correspondence of any hon. member of parliament should not be the subject matter of motions, orders for the production of papers or questions, but I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that we are being victimized very forcefully as individual members of parliament if we must not only face questions and criticism of the government but also of other members of parliament working in co-operation with them for the purpose of eliciting and developing this kind of information. I think we are at the stage where we are likely to move into an extremely bad practice.
I should also like you to look at questions 2,720 to 2,724 inclusive, with regard to which the only explanation I can see is that they have been placed on the order paper by way of harassment of the hon. member for Yukon because of his actions in the past. So far as I am concerned, obviously those questions have been planted by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard for this purpose with the encouragement of someone in the department itself.
I think all members of parliament, whether government or opposition, only ask for a fair chance. After consultation with your officials, Mr. Speaker, who deal with the order paper and questions of procedure, I now put before you for your advice the question whether there is a clear cut case here of collusion of the kind that would attack the traditional parliamentary rights of members of parliament.
If you do not want to take this matter under advisement, Mr. Speaker, and make a report to us, then I am in the position where I feel I have to make a motion. I feel that common

Question of Privilege
courtesy to the house is involved in asking you to take this matter under advisement because the whole matter of questions is handled by you and by your officials working for us. For that reason I would ask you to take the matter under advisement and report back to us what are your observations and what is your view with respect to these questions I have raised. Otherwise I should like the opportunity to make a formal motion at this time.

speechtext: Order, please. I do not think I need any advice in this matter. The question raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur involves a fundamentally important principle, and I certainly accept his suggestion. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur, may I say I think it is unfair to ask the Speaker of the House of Commons to undertake this task. The Speaker of the House of Commons and his officials are responsible for the placing on the order paper of questions and motions for the production of papers. The officials give advice to members as to the wording of questions on some occasions so that we do not fall into the error of putting something on the order paper which is contrary to the rules or is badly phrased.
But the problem raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur is much wider than that. Surely it is no function of the Speaker to ascertain whether or not access to files has been made available to private members of the house. I do not know what sort of investigation Mr. Speaker could carry on in that regard. If I understood the accusation of the hon. member for Port Arthur, it was based more on that ground rather than simply the technical arrangement of questions on the order paper.
Consequently I certainly regret that the hon. member for Port Arthur did not move a motion to refer this matter to the committee on privileges and elections, where the members themselves can deal with a subject that is of great importance to each member of the house. Under the circumstances I would un-

dertake to move such a motion, that the subject matter of the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections.

maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand that Your Honour would like to have the time and opportunity to review the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur before you decide whether there is what we would call a prima facie case of privilege. However, with regard to the problem involved in Your Honour having to judge whether there would appear to be some kind of collusion between an hon. member and officials within the Department of Justice, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that if Your Honour is called upon to make such a judgment it will put you in a very awkward position.
Citation 114 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, in the section dealing with questions of privilege, reads as follows:
Cases may arise of communications, beyond the walls of parliament, between one member and another, or between a member and a minister, so closely related to some matter pending in, or expected to be brought before, the house, that though they do not take place in the chamber or in a committee room, they form part of the business of the house, as, for example, where a member sends to a minister the draft of a question he is thinking of putting down or shows it to another member with a view to obtaining advice as to the propriety of putting it down, or as to the manner in which it should be framed.
I am not going to quote the whole citation, but it very clearly states that if a question of privilege arises out of this kind of situation -and obviously that is what is before the house this afternoon-the house and only the house should deal with a matter of this kind.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree entirely with what the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said. The suggestion made places you in a very unenviable position. Our purpose as members of the house must be at all times to maintain your integrity in the high position you occupy and not to place you in the position of judging whether certain questions that have got on the order paper should not have been placed there on the basis of the rules. Over the years I have had questions turned down that were less informative and knowledgeable in the manner in which they were drafted than those to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Port Arthur.

Indeed, when I think of the question of ethics I would point out that no one feels that members of parliament should in any way be above the law. Under the privileges of parliament no one wants to protect wrongdoing; but certainly if the information that has been given to me is correct, directives have been sent out by a minister within the past several weeks to a number of departments, including Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, asking for information concerning any correspondence or files relating to the hon. member for Yukon.

maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Shame.

I should like to have this matter fully examined, because the Prime Minister himself took a most highminded position in the letter that he wrote to his ministers on December 22 last. I am not going into the full particulars thereof, but in part it reads as follows:
I am therefore writing this letter to ask you, as well as every other minister, to have a meeting at once with your ministerial staff in order to impress on them the vital importance of their conduct. I am following this course in my own office.
In the course of this wise admonition, which apparently has not been too carefully followed since, he went on to say:
I think you should also emphasize the responsibilities that staff members have with regard to official information, whether it is formally classified or not.
I emphasize those words, "whether formally classified or not."
They must not, directly or indirectly, use such information for their own advantage or for that of any friend or associate.
They must also observe rigorously their obligation to maintain the confidentiality of classified information or of information about members of the public that comes to them in the discharge of their official duties.
Now, all these questions that have been referred to by the hon. member in a most impressive presentation, if I may say so, make very clear-

We sincerely believe that you yourself can determine the way in which hon. members have to put their questions and decide what is to be done to change and improve the performance given by the House of Commons at the present time.
I indeed support the hon. member for Port Arthur when he suggests that you should decide upon this matter. The Prime Minister is also of this opinion. On the other hand, we shall take the stand that, under the circumstances, we shall await your decision.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. J. P. Cameron (High Park):

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FRENCH COPY OF PENSION COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron), on a question of privilege which will be found at page 11925 of Hansard, requested information concerning delay in the preparation of the French version of the proceedings of the special joint committee dealing with the Canada pension plan bill.
The facts are as follows. The day to day English proceedings and evidence are forwarded to the bureau for printing. In so far as the printing of the French minutes of proceedings and evidence is concerned, they must first be translated and revised, and as soon as they are ready and received from the translators they are forwarded to the printing bureau.
To date only one number has been translated and printed. This translation was forwarded to the bureau on February 3, 1965 and received and distributed on February 15.

House of Commons
Of the remaining 23 numbers, seven have been translated and are now being revised and will be delivered shortly to the printing bureau. Another 13 are in the process of translation, and three have still to be allocated for translation.
There are no delays between the reception of the translation and the transmittal of the French copy to the printing bureau. The delay for this committee is the same as for every other committee; it is attributable only to the translation. Such delays cannot be avoided because of the shortage of translators and the considerable volume of translations other than minutes and proceedings of evidence which the translators have to do. There is a shortage of competent translators.
I have been in touch with the translation branch and am informed that they are doing their utmost to expedite the translation; and I, of course, know that the printing bureau will do their very best to print it as soon as it is received. The hon. member is not correct in his statement that the French version of the report has not yet been received. When I tabled my report on February 16 the report was in both English and French. It is printed in full in the French version of Votes and Proceedings of that date, commencing at page 1037.
May I add, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Beauce was a member of the select committee of the House of Commons and the Senate dealing with the Canada pension plan bill, and up to the moment he raised his question of privilege in the house he had made no complaint whatsoever to hie about the failure to receive the report in French.

maintopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER
subtopic: REQUEST FOR FRENCH COPY OF PENSION COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
since the question of privilege I raised yesterday is brought up again, and that as a justification it is claimed that the translators were overworked, I would like to point out that the committee sat chiefly during the recess when the translators of the House of Commons could have been assigned to this committee, in order to produce rapidly an urgently needed French translation of the proceedings of the committee.
Such an excuse cannot be accepted by those who wish to obtain the French version of the deliberations of that committee which held 51 meetings before the resumption of the session on February 16 last. Therefore, translators could have been available to translate the discussions which were held

in English in that committee. We can definitely not accept that excuse that easily.
When I claim that we do not have all the necessary documents and tools, that is, the French version of the proceedings of that committee-and after all, there are 13 members who belong to the Ralliement Creditiste and I was their only representative on that committee-I believe that I am right and that many more like myself would have liked to have a translation of those proceedings on this bill, which will be passed even before we receive that version.
Therefore, the so-called excuse profferred today to justify the delay in this French translation is definitely not acceptable.

subtopic: SUBSIDIES ON WOODEN FISHING VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member
[Mr. Favreau.l

knows, for some years the construction of fishing vessels of over 100 gross tons has been assisted through the ship construction assistance program administered by the Canadian maritime commission under the Department of Transport. Construction of smaller fishing vessels has been assisted through a program administered by the Department of Fisheries.
In a move to co-ordinate these two programs after April 1, assistance in the construction of wooden fishing vessels over 100 tons will be handled by the Department of Fisheries. speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend knows that in this case the Winnipeg Tribune is completely in error. It copied part of a story, which was one of the most surprising I have ever seen, in the Toronto Telegram, in which many of the quotes ascribed to me contained things I did not even know about until I read them in the newspaper. I have told one of the Winnipeg newspapers which has given prominence to my statement, that I denied ever saying I did not want the games in Winnipeg.
Indeed, as I pointed out and as my hon. friend knows, I did send officials out there. We have been working with the people in Winnipeg for some time. I went out myself expressly for that purpose on the way back from the Churchill funeral, to discuss and assist the city of Winnipeg in the proposal which it has followed for some six years. My hon. friend knows also, as I said before in the house, that we more than doubled the offer of the previous government in a very generous arrangement. It has been our hope that Winnipeg will have the games.
I admit quite frankly that I did state in a spirit of joshing to Mayor Juba, and subsequently I am sure to anyone else who listened, that Canada was going to have the Pan-Am games even if I had to have them built in Niagara Falls. However, I expect they are going to be in Winnipeg.

May I ask
a supplementary question. How much money has the federal government now pledged to the city of Winnipeg as its contribution to the Pan-Am games?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. As was stated before, we have offered the sum of $1 million, more than twice the originally pledged $460,000. In addition, as the authorities understand, there will have to be assistance from the federal government, very likely through the Department of National Defence, with respect to housing many of the officials. We have offered the assistance of the Department of National Health and Welfare in order to get preparation for the games started as quickly as possible, and in order that Canada will be proud of the contribution which will be made by Winnipeg in holding these games.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPORT ON POLICE ACTIVITIES DURING ROYAL VISIT TO QUEBEC
speechtext:
The member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked whether I had now received an R.C.M.P. report regarding certain allegations of excessive brutality by the police during disturbances in Quebec city at the time of the royal visit and whether I would make its contents available to members of the house.
The hon. member for Lapointe asked whether the R.C.M.P. was in charge of all police forces that day and had urged certain measures on the Quebec city police.
I am afraid that a little misunderstanding has crept into the question of such a report by the R.C.M.P. and in order to clear it up and reply to the questions, I must refer back to October 22, 1964, when the hon. member for Lapointe asked whether I had asked for a report on the events which took place on the day in question and, more specifically, on the behaviour of members of the local police forces. I replied to the effect that I would make a statement the next day.
On the next day, October 23, 1964, I did make a fairly detailed statement based upon

facts reported to me by the R.C.M.P., and I would refer hon. members to that statement.
I said that "the prime responsibility of the R.C.M.P. was for the safety of Her Majesty and His Royal Highness and that a second responsibility was to furnish assistance to municipal and provincial police in the event that, in the maintenance of law and order, those forces required assistance. And I elaborated further the events of the day.
Then on November 13, 1964, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked me again whether I had received a report from the R.C.M.P. regarding the activities of the police in general in Quebec city, on the occasion of the royal visit. I replied I had not yet received such a report, and, when it was received, a decision would be made on whether to make it public.
In the meantime I have had oral discussions with the R.C.M.P. in which they have explained to me further the part they played in connection with the royal visit, but they have not made me a further written report. I consider that the part played by the R.C.M.P. was quite fully covered in the statement which I made on October 23, 1964, on the basis of the report made to me at that time, and there is nothing I could usefully add to this statement, with the exception of the following.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Lapointe I can say that the security measures taken by the R.C.M.P. concerned directly the personal security of Her Majesty and Prince Philip. However, the maintenance of good order and peace in the city of Quebec were the responsibility of the municipal police, with the assistance of the Quebec provincial police, and the R.C.M.P. were not in charge of those police forces in the execution of their duties and did not, of course, give them orders as to how their duties were to be performed.
The R.C.M.P. ought to be commended foi the way in which it carried on its duties on the occasion of the royal visit both in Quebec city and elsewhere in Canada, and I would wish that all parties would join in acknowledging that, on that occasion, that great Canadian force has once more conducted itself in accordance with the sacred principles of its proud tradition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I wish to make a comment on the lending of this money to the provinces. So far as nine provinces are concerned the fund may build up to $8 billion in 1985, and including Quebec the total could add up to something like $11 billion during the next 20 years. It seems to me that if the decision were made to have a partially funded plan, at least a plan building up a fund of this magnitude, then here was an excellent opportunity to use this fund to solve some of the national problems. As it is, there are no strings attached to the manner in which the provinces may use this money. They can use it in any way they wish. It is true certain provinces may have particular problems which they would like to solve. But the government has repeatedly said this is a national plan; so we had an opportunity, if it had been devised in a different way, to have built up a large fund to be used for national purposes. We could have said: We have a large sum of money available to the provinces but we recognize that such and such is a national problem. It could be the renovation of metropolitan areas, for example, or it could have been the preservation of our water resources.
I think the government has missed an opportunity of using this very large fund to solve some of our national problems, and though some of them might have concerned areas within the responsibility of the provinces, yet by the inducement of offering lower interest rates with respect to certain favoured projects a good deal might have been accomplished. It would have been necessary, of course, to have devised the plan in a different way. To sum up, I believe the government has missed an excellent opportunity to use this large fund to solve some of our national problems in Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I asked this question in the committee-I am not sure whether it arises under this clause or not-but I do not recall whether any satisfactory answer was given to me. Canada Pension Plan

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Perhaps I might make a comment at this point. After money is lent to governments, whether provincial or municipal, those governments spend it. So a situation might arise some time in the future, should the fund have been depleted rapidly, when there was need for a sudden call on the provinces to fulfil these obligations. What would happen if there were a serious recession in a particular province; the province has spent the money lent to it, and suddenly the federal government calls upon it to repay the funds. In such a case political pressure would be brought to bear on the federal government to defer the call for repayment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: The security which the federal government has in making these loans is, of course, limited to the financial credit of the province concerned. It is usually considered a pretty good investment. When funds are advanced to a province the province concerned is fully aware that there is a maturity date and that it must be in a position to return the funds in the same way as if it had gone to the market and borrowed money. Thus, when the date arrives for the funds to be paid back to the plan-and as I mentioned, this is anticipated at the end of a 20 year period. If at that time this parliament and the provinces in their wisdom decide that the fund is to be kept at a certain level, they would also have to face the prospect of effecting an increase in contributions to the plan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I might point out that there is a big difference between provinces borrowing on the open market and borrowing from the federal government. In the latter case the question of political pressure always arises on certain occasions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Under the Canada pension plan, no political pressure could be exercised by any individual province with regard to loans. They have an entitlement based upon a ten year moving average of contributions and that is all they are entitled to. I might point out that from figures I have seen the size of the loan available to any province even on the basis of the most optimistic view would be

Canada Pension Plan
nowhere close to the amount provinces are currently borrowing each year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: The minister has not answered the exact question put by the hon. member a moment ago regarding what would happen in the event of a prolonged recession leading to a state of emergency or of incapacity within the provincial administrations, as was the case in the years 1933, 1934 and 1935, when certain provinces were unable to meet their normal obligations and had to hand over certain responsibilities-in the field of unemployment for instance-to the federal government? maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
We all realize the great responsibility which is imposed on trustees in connection with any private pension plan. Funds built up under such plans are almost the most sacrosanct of investment funds. This is because the moneys belong to private individuals and have been laid aside for their future. It has been suggested in a number of circles that this is one area in which the Canada pension plan is not as strong as it might be, inasmuch as the provinces, being
[Mr. Benson.1
able to borrow this money on the strength of their credit reputation, would have no greater responsibility with regard to these funds than they would have with regard to any other type of obligation.
I know the provinces do regard their credit responsibilities seriously, but we have known it to happen that there have been defaults. There have been difficulties. One can foresee the possibility, say 15 or 20 years hence, of a province being in economic difficulty, and unable to honour its commitments and bonded obligations toward the Canada pension plan. What safeguard is there; because provincial governments are administered by men, subject to human frailties.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

There are the pension
trustees.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

Yes, Mr. Chairman, but we have reinforced these by certain much more stringent regulations as to the type of investments they can make, so that the fund is in a liquid position. We know that the provinces may borrow this money for expenditure in fields of their own choice. They may be self-liquidating; they may be for general purposes. Yet there is the temptation at the provincial level to perhaps enter into a form of expenditure which may be politically, publicly or popularly expedient and which would be really an unwise investment from the province's point of view, bearing in mind the source of its money, because it must be refunded.
It is not like, say, provincial revenues which are obtained on current account, and if they are spent not as wisely as they might be, well that is a mistake. But moneys do not have to be found to be refunded. Yet with regard to the pension fund moneys, they must be available at all times; any expenditures of these moneys by the provinces must be repaid to the Canada pension plan. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I am wondering what particular safeguards there are, other than the normal honesty and judgment of provincial government officials. What safeguards is the federal government going to rely on for its Canada pension plan?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the security behind loans to provinces-I refer to federal government loans to the provinces-is of course the credit of the province and the ability of the province to repay these debts through taxation of its people. This is exactly the same security that is behind any of the securities issued by a province. My hon. friend spoke of trustees. Generally, provincial gov-

ernment securities are trustee investments; trustees of pension funds can invest in provincial government securities. The federal government, in spreading this out on the basis of contribution across the nine provinces in Canada which will be in this plan, presumably, is spreading the risk right across the whole country. I would say that from the point of view of the trustees, if one was a trustee of a pension fund this would be a good diversification of a risk in investing in government bonds. As my hon. friend pointed out, we have to rely on the liquidity and ability of the province to repay these funds through taxation, which ultimately they must do; because just as they go out and borrow in the open market now, they must consider whether or not they will be able to repay in the long run out of the amounts they can raise in taxation within the province, which of course includes the equalization of federal taxes, which is money coming into the provincial coffers as well.
I think this is pretty good security. In addition to this, under the Canada pension plan the federal government is required to get an actuarial report every five years in order to bring up to date the actuarial estimates of the department of insurance in connection with the operation of the pension plan over the next number of years. This might in itself, perhaps five years hence, provide a warning signal as to what is going to happen to the funds. I think the federal government will make full use of this in forecasting its investment policy beyond the five-year period. If one found the funds were not going to build up so fast, or the Minister of Finance really needed more than a three months pay-out in his hands, this matter could be put up to the provinces. But the security behind these investments is the credit rating of all the provinces in Canada, just the same as securities issued by the government of Canada are backed by the credit rating of the government of Canada, which ultimately depends on its ability to tax. Therefore I believe the security is really quite good, and I think it would be acceptable to any trustee in the pension plan.

speechtext:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

maintopic: THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF DENTISTS OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I only wish to say a few words on Bill No. S-44.

In view of the fact that bills concerning professional organizations have already been dealt with in this house, and that some members objected to the adoption of those bills because to a certain extent they did not affect the province of Quebec, I must say that since this bill was introduced in the Senate, I have received no representations whatsoever against the passing of this bill. Furthermore, one of the provisional directors is Dr. Remi Langlois, a dentist from Quebec city, who apparently seems to endorse the creation of this new royal college of dentists of Canada.
I was a little concerned because I wondered if this college of dentists intended to license those professionals to practise dental surgery in the different provinces. After glancing through this bill, I find that such is not the case. Consequently, I believe that the jurisdiction of the provinces is not at stake and that such jurisdiction was not overstepped. I do not see why we would object to this bill, because its purpose is to recognize the qualifications of dentists who became specialists after obtaining their diploma and the right to practise in various provinces. Therefore, I do not believe that we should object to it since there already exists for the medical profession a royal college which grants special titles and qualifications to those who have pursued special studies and are particularly qualified, and since those new titles are recognized by the province of Quebec. I do not see why we should object to the granting of the same privileges to the college of dentists.
However, I wish to point out that the college of physicians in the province of Quebec, has set some specialization standards of its own and it grants certificates to its members who have attended the necessary classes and who have been in practice for the required number of years. speakeroldname: Mr. S. Perry Ryan (for Mr. Wahn) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-42, respecting Interprovincial Pipe Line Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company was originally incorporated by the parliament of Canada in the year 1949. The purpose of this bill is to subdivide each of the 40 million authorized shares of the par value of $5 each of the capital stock of the company into five shares of the par value of $1 each. This is a public company and this stock split is sought to encourage purchase of the company stock by small Canadian investors and also to enable the company's employees to become shareholders more easily.
Although par value of a common share is at present $5, the current market value is somewhere around $93.50. This high price for one share greatly discourages purchases of shares by small investors. The company finds that on the market its shares are for the most part bought and sold by investment funds and syndicates which buy and sell in large blocks. This causes somewhat inordinate fluctuations in the company's stock from day to day on the market. There may be changes of $3, $4 or $5 a day as a result of these big purchases and sales.
There are at present between 12,000 and 13,000 shareholders in the company and from the share register of the company it would appear that currently about 88 per cent of the outstanding stock is held by Canadians and
Private Bills
Canadian corporations. You will appreciate that the stock split that the company seeks will have the effect of greatly increasing the number of shareholders, particularly among small Canadian investors. The individual at the present time, for about $1,000, would only be able to acquire 10 shares whereas after the proposed stock split he would be able to acquire approximately 50 shares for $1,000. Those who have had any dealings in the stock market will realize that it is often easier to get a sale for 50 shares than it is for 10 shares without having to take a discount.
I have no personal interest in this company whatsoever. In fact, I am acting on behalf of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) in this matter this afternoon and he has assured me he also has no personal interest in the company whatsoever. This company has been very successful and has been phenomenally successful in reducing by 42 per cent the cost of moving oil by pipe line. It does not buy or sell oil at all. It simply provides a service through western Canada, the northern states of the United States, around the south end of lake Huron and into Ontario at Sarnia for the movement of oil and allied products from our western fields.
During the company's existence its tariffs have come down steadily. It always was much cheaper to move oil by pipe line than by rail, but this company has demonstrated that it can move oil far more economically than was originally anticipated. The company is at present subject to regulation by the national energy board. It must ship for owners at published tariff rates which are filed with the board, and the board makes a constant study of the company's rates. The directors and officials of the corporation are all Canadian citizens.
I would ask that this bill be given second reading and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines as is customary with pipe line bills, which are considered quite analogous to railway bills.
I should like to ask the hon. member one question. How many of the shares have been issued out of the treasury?

About one eighth of the shares. About $25 million worth of stock has been issued and about $175 million is unissued. There are 40 million shares at a par value of $5 and if you divide the par value figure

Private Bills
into $25 million that will give the number of shares.
I just want to ask a question. Am I to understand that the par value of the stock at this date is $5 a share?
The par value, yes; but the market value is approximately $93.50, just under 19 times the par value.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly would not wish to accuse the member who is proposing second reading of the bill of having cribbed the speech he has just made, but I must say that the speech I listened to, in which he outlined the reasons for the proposal to split the shares of this company, almost completely resembled a speech I heard on another occasion in this house. The speech of which I was reminded was made before the hon. member was a member of the house, I believe, and had to do with a bill to split the shares of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company with which this house was asked to deal a number of years ago.
I do not know that I am prepared to oppose second reading of the bill and having it referred to the standing committee, but I must say that the arguments and reasons he advanced for the proposal to split these shares, and his great solicitude that small investors should have an opportunity to acquire stock in the company do not sound any more convincing to me than the similar arguments I heard advanced in respect of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company years ago. I think most members realize that in relatively recent years there has been a great development in the construction of pipe lines for the purpose of the transmission of oil and gas from various places to various places throughout the country. This development has probably been a very valuable and worth while one so far as our economy is concerned. I am just saying, however, that there are some members in this house who are and have been a bit concerned about the arrangements under which these pipe line companies have been enabled to operate in a way that has made this business one that is lucrative almost without parallel in the economic development of our country.
We are concerned that this has resulted in a higher price for gas, oil and other petroleum products to the consumers of Canada. I think this question is tied in with the fact that shares which were issued at a par value of $5 are now, according to the explanatory note, quoted at approximately $85 or $85.50

each. Apparently in the interval since the bill was introduced in the Senate, the shares have risen to something over $90, if I heard the member correctly. I must say that this argument, that the splitting of shares will make shares more easily available to small investors, has not been very well borne out by the facts, so far as I know, in cases where the shares have been split. I think that in many cases over the years it has been proven that the real motivation behind this desire to split shares is to enable some of these companies to conceal successfully the rate of profit they are making upon the investment and upon the operation of their undertaking.
Some of us might be a little happier if some of those concerned who come forward with bills and advance this innocuous proposal in respect of their desire to split shares, would be quite blunt and frank about telling us why they want to split the shares. These are some of the questions that flashed through my mind immediately on hearing the hon. member who introduced this bill. He made a speech which, as I suggested, was virtually identical to the speech which was made from that side of the house by the hon. member who introduced the bill concerning the share splitting proposal of Trans Mountain Pipe Line a number of years ago. Certainly I, for one, hope that this bill goes before a committee where it will receive careful attention and examination from the point of view of determining why this proposal to split the shares is placed before this house. I hope the representatives of this concern, who I presume will be asked to appear before the committee, will be prepared to give some detailed information and be ready to offer explanations in considerable detail and depth about the operations of this company.
I may add, Mr. Speaker, that I hope they may be able to present somewhat more convincing and substantial arguments than the representatives of Trans Mountain Pipe Line were able to do when they appeared in a somewhat similar role a number of years ago.

We in this party realize what is being asked for in this bill is not something unique. It has been done before in this parliament in respect of companies that required a federal charter, and it has been done quite often for companies who are operating under provincial charter as well. We are not certain that there is a need to split the stock of this company. However, it seems to me that it is not our responsibility

to oppose this request, if it happens to be the wish of the majority of the shareholders in a corporation as expressed through the board of directors.
One point I do want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that I would not like the hon. member who has made a speech outlining some of the reasons for requesting this split to think we are so naive that we would accept some of the arguments he has advanced on behalf of small investors. He said that the market value of the shares is now $93.50. Someone who had $935 to invest at the present time could only buy ten shares. If this bill passes, the company will be granted permission to make a five to one split, and then the small investor in Canada would be able to buy 50 shares for $935.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like the hon. member who made that suggestion to show us one case in which a company has made a stock split when that has been the case. The minute a company gives an indication that a stock split is imminent, there is a rush in the market which forces up the price of such shares. What is more, following the split, there is never, so far as I know, a re-evaluation of the shares on the market that reflects the proportion of the stock split. So, Mr. Speaker, I would not like the hon. member to think we are so naive that we accept this kind of argument.
The second point is this: I should like to know, some time before this bill gets through all its stages, how much of the authorized 40 million shares have been issued? The hon. member said that it would be about 25 million.
If the hon. member will permit me, I can give him the figures. I have them here.

I am not sure it would be proper for the sponsor to intercede in this debate again. I would not mind, but I believe there are some other members who want to speak as well.
In any event, I should like to know how many of these shares have been issued. I should like to know also if they were all sold for $5 per share, that is if all those that have been issued out of the treasury have been sold for $5. If they have not, then the mathematics that have been put before us have no basis. They do not stand up. We do know that Imperial Oil Company of Canada is the major shareholder. I should like to know how many shares they hold. I have no objection to a Canadian company, even though it is a sub-20220-758
Private Bills
sidiary of another company, getting into the shares of a company that is actually in a position to benefit Canada. I should like to know, because there is no doubt in my mind that if this split becomes a fact, all the existing shareholders are going to realize a tremendous increment in the value of the shares they now hold. This may not be something to be resisted completely but, for example, if one shareholder holds something like 30 per cent of the shares then I am fairly sure a real bonanza will be realized on the market from this split.
If the company requires further financing and wishes to secure it on the basis of issuing more shares out of the treasury it has certainly sufficient room within the existing provisions of the charter to do so, and might perhaps sell them for something like $90. I do not accept the argument that this will be particularly good for the small investors. It will be good for investors of all magnitude. We do not oppose the bill being sent to committee but these are some of the questions which we shall be asking.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house long but, like my colleague from Comox-Alberni, I was struck by the similarity of this measure to the one we dealt with some years ago. Until the speech of the hon. member who has just finished, I was not aware that this particular company is in precisely the same position with the Imperial Oil Company as was the other one.
On that previous occasion I tried to seek information from officers of the company, and I may say they advanced the same arguments which the hon. member advanced. I tried to get answers to two questions that had to be answered before one could judge the desirability of the move. My first question was whether the company was proposing to release shares now held in the company treasury to employees who wished to buy shares in the company that employs them? My second question was, failing that were the directors prepared to put some of their own shares on the market, or did they know of any shareholders who were prepared to do that?
In both cases the answer I got was no, which to me seemed conclusive evidence that the expressed purpose of the bill at that time was not the real reason for it, because it was perfectly obvious that unless they were prepared to release shares held in the treasury, or unless the directors were prepared to sell

Private Bills
some of their holdings, there were not going to be any of these split shares available for purchase by the small investor. I would like to be assured of that before this bill passes third reading.
I am interested in this bill because there is special mention made of an employees' savings fund, and that they are to have an option of investing their planned savings in the stock of the company at current market prices. What I want to know is, are the directors of this company making sure there will be shares available to be purchased by the employees when the shares are split five to one as proposed by the bill?
I hope the sponsor of the bill will instruct the witnesses who are to appear before the committee on the necessity of answering these questions fully and completely if they want to satisfy the members of the house that this is a desirable piece of legislation.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

I have a number of questions I should like to ask in respect of this clause, Mr. Chairman.
This clause deals with the opting out provisions of provinces subsequent to the adoption of this bill. of Dominion of Canada securities, is that correct?

Mr. Chairman, this brings up a question which has puzzled me for some time. I have read with some care the transcript of the proceedings of the committee. Unfortunately I was not one of those privileged to serve on the committee during the recess but I did take the time to read the reports. What concerns me is this. Obviously section 114 applies in a situation where a province has, under section 3, introduced a plan which is to all intents and purposes comparable with the national pension plan.
I think we must envisage a situation where some province may at some time wish to introduce a different plan. As you know, sometimes political parties seeking power think it is advantageous for them to make suggestions as to introducing pension plans of one kind or another. This sometimes yields political benefits. We may find an opposition party saying in the course of a provincial election campaign that they have a far better plan providing for smaller contributions by employers or employees and possibly, with careful management and manipulation, also providing for larger benefits. They may undertake to put such a plan into effect in two years and they may be elected.
Assuming they implement their election promise and introduce a plan which is not comparable and which, instead of a 1.8 contribution, provides for a smaller contribution and larger benefits, if that might be mathematically possible at some time in the future, then would this not be a situation where the plan of the province would not be comparable to the national pension plan? Under those conditions section 94A of the British North America Act comes into force and, as the minister understands, it provides that no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law, present or future, of a provincial legislature.
It is my submission that if a plan such as I have mentioned, not comparable to the national plan, was enacted by a provincial legislature, that plan is bound to be affected by the federal plan because it will provide for contributions and benefits on a different scale and therefore, within the meaning of section 94A, it must affect the provincial plan. The national plan affects the provincial plan. What then is the situation?

I know that the minister may well say that this is hypothetical, that the plan we now have before us is such a good plan that no province is likely to attempt to alter or vary it. But we cannot take action today on that basis. This is a very distinct possibility in the course of time and perhaps in the not too distant future. What then will be the situation vis-a-vis securities? What will be the situation with regard to employers, employees and recipients? What will be their rights in the case of a province which takes such action?
This is a matter which has puzzled me. I read with some care the very useful evidence given by the person who drafted the bill. He attempted to deal with this point. I think he suggested you would first have to have a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to decide if the two schemes were comparable. I am suggesting that the schemes could not be comparable, that if there was a difference in contributions or a difference in benefits the federal plan would cease to affect the people of that province. This is a situation which might well come about, having regard to the state of this country. What would be the situation with regard to the recipients, the contributors and the funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very interesting possibility raised by my friend, but I think it is a pretty remote one. I ask the committee to consider what the situation would be, for instance, 10 years from now. The people of Canada will have a considerable investment in their own pension plan. The plan will be in operation and will be a well accepted and well liked part of the social fabric of the country. It may well be that my hon. friend knows something about the similar plan in the United States and how thoroughly it is woven into the fabric of that nation.
It is true there is no way in which the federal government could prohibit any provincial government from introducing a totally dissimilar plan and perhaps might not be able to persuade it not to do so. However, my friend is a well experienced and skilful lawyer who has looked at the phraseology of the amendment to the British North America Act and may know that there is some conflict of opinion as to which of the jurisdictions has priority. May I suggest to him that if there is a scheme in operation 10 or 20 years from now which has a contribution rate of 3.6 per cent and another jurisdiction decides to impose a new and dissimilar scheme, despite the confusion that will be engendered,

this to be added on top, it might not be very well received by the individuals of that province. All other things apart, it might be a considerable political problem for the province concerned. It might very well be that there would have to be litigation; I do not know. In any event, there would certainly be consultation and there would be great difficulty in bringing in a very dissimilar plan when this plan has been in operation for some years.
It was for this reason, I think, that all provinces took such a tremendous interest in this legislation and so many dominion-provincial meetings were held with such deep and detailed discussion. While what the hon. member has suggested remains a possibility- considering the nature of the legislation and the nature of politics and indeed the fact that people have a comfortable feeling when they know what their future holds so far as social legislation is concerned-considering all these factors I suggest it is highly unlikely that anything will be done and it is not something for which this committee can make adequate preparation now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I think the minister has given the best answer she can. I do not think anything else can be said. However, I would be derelict in my duty if I did not bring this matter to the attention of the house and indicate that this probability does exist. I emphasize that last June the same thought occurred to me so I asked the Prime Minister a question on orders of the day. I asked him if he did not think it would be far more satisfactory to have attempted to secure, in view of this co-operation that existed between the provinces and the federal government, a consequential amendment to section 94A which would have settled this matter beyond any doubt and placed in the hands of the federal government the primary responsibility which I think is probably necessary to effectively discharge the duty of any government which attempts to implement a national pension plan.
Now, let me just make one more statement here. There was one problem I mentioned which I believe the minister failed to understand as I heard her answer. If a province introduced a plan that was not comparable, the political consequences to any government of that province may be disastrous because the people would be faced with the cumulative effect of the two plans. If you carefully read, and take a logical interpretation of section 94A, that is not the case, especially when you read these words:
Canada Pension Plan
-but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
The only meaning you can derive from that is that once a province does legislate a plan which is not comparable, automatically the federal legislation has no effect in that province. The primary responsibility then falls upon the province. This would be the effect of section 94A in a situation of that kind. The federal legislation would not apply at all because it would then be a case where the federal legislation was affecting the operation of a provincial scheme, and therefore the provincial scheme only would be in effect, not the federal scheme. Under those conditions, what happens to the pensions of the Canadian contributors, what happens to the funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The constitutional argument is a perfectly respectable one as put forward by my friend. He made the suggestion that perhaps this matter might have been clarified in order to give jurisdiction to one authority. I must say that this idea occurred to a lot of people at the time, but the 11 governments were not unanimous on this question. The interpretation that he has placed upon the section is very well recognized and one made by very many constitutional lawyers.
However, there are opposite opinions quite violently disagreeing with this interpretation. There are constitutional lawyers who are of the opinion that the federal government, once in the field, has, in effect, occupied it. It is not my role, at this juncture in my life, to choose between those opinions. This second opinion was given by no less an august personage than Mr. Bora Laskin, of the University of Toronto, who was my professor of constitutional law. He holds very strongly to the view that, if federal legislation were there, it would take priority over provincial legislation.
Be that as it may, I hope, and fully expect, we will never find out which particular view is correct. One thing would have to be borne in mind should such a tragedy come to pass, and that is that those individuals of Canada who were a part of the plan, who had made their contributions, and indeed probably made other private financial arrangements to fit in with the anticipated benefits for their retirement years, would have to be guaranteed by the federal government, preferably in cooperation with the province or even without that co-operation, that the benefits which they had already accumulated would not be lost.

Canada Pension Plan
This is a pension plan which, it can be appreciated, becomes a pledge of the country to the people that their accumulation of pension contributions will never be lost. I would not want to think any member of the public might be alarmed into believing that at some future time all this might come to pass and their money would have gone for nothing. As I said to my hon. friend, it is a valid objection, it is a valid argument. However, I feel that in view of all the considerations, it is highly unlikely, and not a matter for anyone to feel disquieted about.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is interesting to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare explain, with all the eloquence she can muster, that one or more provinces can join the plan and other provinces can opt out. According to her every province in Canada, except Quebec, naturally, are satisfied with the federal government's pension plan.
I have just returned from a trip to western Canada where I had the opportunity of meeting people in Winnipeg, Edmonton and in every western province, and these people are doing their utmost to deride the government's pension plan.
The authorities in British Columbia, where the old age pension is the same as in Quebec and the other provinces, decided to add $30 to the pension of $75 a month. As a matter of fact, such action was proposed to the British Columbia legislature in Victoria. Old people will therefore get a pension of $105 a month, without a means test at 70 and with a means test at 65.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder on what ground the Minister of National Health and Welfare stands when she says that the provinces as a whole are pleased with the pension plan. In fact, in one province legislation is enacted, in another province another piece of legislation is enacted, and here we have a bill so thick that even the most thick-headed will be unable to understand the first word of it. Why should we keep on discussing, when the provinces can manage their own business alone without any interference whatsoever from the Minister of National Health and Welfare?
If British Columbia can enact legislation without the help of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, if Quebec can opt out of the Canada pension plan and if the premier of Manitoba, Mr. Roblin, has indicated that he would rather not join the Canada pension
[Miss LaMarsh.l
plan, why should we keep up our consideration and discussion about a pension plan that the provinces do not seem prepared to join? That is what I would like the Minister of National Health and Welfare to explain clearly at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is most unfortunate that after the house unanimously passed a resolution that it was in favour of the principle, we now find we have a member who is not in favour of it. subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: May I correct the minister. I was listening to the hon. member speaking in French and also listening to the translation. I think there was an error in translation. The reference was to the possibility of Manitoba wishing to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: That means the provinces have to choose a plan that will be approved by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. What if a provincial plan is better than the one we have got? speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: My hon. friend has just come in, but we have been discussing this for some length of time. Clause 114, which we are now considering, does not apply to Quebec; it applies to a province which is in the plan and subsequently decides to go out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Supposing a province does opt out and decides to get its contributions according to residence and not according to where a person is employed? speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: It would not be deemed to be a comparable plan. You would have all sorts of anomalies; some people would be double contributing, and some people would be completely omitted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:

Would the federal government consider the possibility of keeping its fingers out of these situations if, for example, a person residing in Ontario decides to move out? premier might decide that his province should have their own plan. If that happened, what would be the position in regard to this plan? I think the minister will find that some premiers might possibly be stubborn in this regard, and it might mean that a person who had been contributing would be caught between two fires and would be paying in both places.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

Canada Pension Plan

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there are two alternatives open to the government in respect of this pension plan. Either it will be based on place of employment or place of residence. subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
